Kofi locked the shop door.

He did it with the slow, deliberate care of a man who had decided, against better judgment, that the world was about to become someone else’s problem inside his walls. The brass key scraped once in the lock. Then he pulled down the blinds and turned the OPEN sign face in, as if the small red word itself might start asking questions.

The stranger stood in the middle of the shop without shifting his weight. He seemed perfectly content to let the room be afraid of him.

Mara, who had spent her life dealing with men who thought stillness was authority, folded her arms and said, “You can start by telling me what you are.”

The man’s mouth twitched, which might have been amusement.

“Kofi,” he said, ignoring her, “you still keep the good thread in the left drawer?”

Kofi stared at him. “I asked you first.”

“Of course you did.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is if you know me.”

“I don’t.”

The stranger looked almost offended by that. Then he sighed, as if correcting a small but embarrassing oversight.

“My name is Anansi.”

Mara blinked.

Kofi made the sign against bad luck with the hand he hoped no one had seen.

Anansi watched him with infuriating calm. “You may say the rest out loud if it helps.”

“You’re dead,” Kofi said.

“Sometimes.”

Mara looked from one to the other. “I’m sorry. Is this a joke? Because I do not have the patience for a religious prank in the middle of my workday.”

“No prank,” Anansi said. “Though I admit I prefer your tone when it is less hostile.”

“His tone is always hostile,” Kofi muttered.

Anansi’s gaze shifted to Mara. “You noticed the shoes.”

“I noticed they were weird.”

“Good. The world is still salvageable.”

“Was that supposed to reassure me?”

“It was supposed to be true.”

Mara pinched the bridge of her nose. “Fine. Let’s say I believe you for the length of this conversation. Why are gods in my shoe repair shop asking for help?”

Anansi’s smile thinned. He seemed to consider whether to answer honestly or entertainingly. Eventually he chose something that looked like both.

“Because one pair of sneakers has gone missing, and because some things break in the wrong place if no one watches them.”

Kofi snorted. “That’s not how shoes work.”

“It is with the shoes I mean.”

Anansi moved to the repair tray on the bench and picked up the damaged black pair with two fingers. Mara expected the shoes to weigh nothing, or to shudder, or to crackle with some obvious magic. Instead they looked badly worn and stubbornly ordinary, except for the way the room seemed to tighten around them.

“These,” he said, “were made to carry a door.”

Kofi frowned. “A door.”

“A threshold, if you want the polite word.”

Mara looked at him. “That’s still not a sensible explanation.”

“No,” Anansi said. “It’s a true one.”

He set the shoes back down. One of the soles had split almost to the toe. The seam was lifting. The damage made Mara uncomfortable in a way she could not explain. It was the kind of damage that, in an ordinary shoe, meant overuse. In this shoe, it felt like an absence.

Anansi noticed her staring and said, “You can tell by looking, can’t you?”

“Tell what?”

“That something has been walking too hard for too long.”

Mara’s mouth opened and then closed again. Because he was right, and because she hated that he was right.

Kofi cleared his throat. “If somebody took your threshold shoes, why come here?”

Anansi gave him a long, unreadable look. “Because you mend what people pretend is beyond repair.”

Kofi’s expression didn’t change, but Mara could see the effect of the words on him. It was too close to flattery to trust and too close to truth to ignore.

Anansi continued, “And because the pair I lost was not the only one. Something is happening to the roads between places. The old ways have become thin.”

Mara let out a sharp breath through her nose. “You are not making this better.”

“I have never been accused of that.”

He walked the length of the shop while speaking, hands folded behind his back. He did not look at the shoes on the shelves, yet everything about him suggested he was counting them.

“Some of us,” he said, “can cross where mortals cannot. Some of us cross because mortals keep making crossings. Roads. Bridges. Stairwells. Tracks. Lines. Shoes are not decoration where I come from, Mara. They are part of the agreement.”

She looked at him coldly. “You keep saying things like I’m supposed to understand them.”

“I keep saying things like I’m hoping you will.”

Kofi set Mara’s sneaker down more carefully than before. “What happens if the agreement is broken?”

Anansi stopped pacing.

For a second, the room changed. Mara couldn’t say how. The air seemed to become thicker at the edges, as though the shop were now balanced on something narrow and invisible.

“When the right shoes go missing,” Anansi said, “the wrong places open.”

No one spoke.

Outside, a delivery truck rattled past in the street, its brakes whining. A siren passed farther away. Ordinary city sounds pressed against the closed glass. Inside, the silence felt crowded.

Mara frowned. “Why us?”

Anansi looked at her as though she had finally asked the most reasonable question in the room. “Because you saw me before I introduced myself. Because Kofi sees what breaks before it falls apart. Because I need people who do not immediately kneel, scream, or run.”

Mara almost laughed. “That’s a very specific hiring standard.”

“Yes.”

Kofi crossed his arms. “And if we say no?”

Anansi shrugged. “Then I continue looking. But by the time I find the shoes, something else may have already taken their place.”

“That sounds like a threat,” Mara said.

“It is a description.”

She stared at him. There was something almost irritatingly human in the way he stood there—patient, infuriating, a little too sure that if he waited long enough the room would bend around him. But there was also something older, deeper, not cruel exactly but unconcerned with the scale of human inconvenience.

Mara looked down at her own sneaker. The heel seam was split. The shoe felt suddenly less like a worn object and more like a promise she had been making to herself without knowing it.

“You said your shoes carry a door,” she said. “What door?”

Anansi’s expression shifted, minutely. “The one between where people are and where they think they are.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the best one you’ll get without a better question.”

Kofi gave a short, tired laugh that held no joy in it. “You always were impossible.”

“And you always were useful.”

“That’s not a compliment.”

“It wasn’t meant to be.”

Mara watched them, trying to decide whether they were old enemies or old friends or simply two beings who had spent enough centuries near each other to become allergic to politeness.

Anansi turned to her again.

“Someone took the pair from the eastern crossing,” he said. “Not all of them. Just enough to make the path misbehave. Since then, there have been reports. Doors that open into empty rooms. Staircases that end where walls should be. Messages delivered to people who have been dead for years.”

Mara went still. “Dead?”

“Yes.”

Kofi muttered, “That’s unfortunate.”

Anansi continued, “And last night, a train arrived at the terminus with no one aboard except a woman wearing red shoes and crying black water.”

Mara felt a chill run down her back that had nothing to do with the shop’s air conditioning.

“Why tell us that?” she asked.

“Because the missing shoes are not merely missing. They are being used.”

Kofi frowned. “By whom?”

Anansi’s eyes moved to the window, as if he could see through the blinds, through the street, through the city itself to something else waiting there.

“That,” he said, “is what I need you to help me discover.”

He reached into his coat and drew out a single shoelace.

It was white, but not clean white. Not synthetic white. Something older had made it that color. It lay across his palm like a thread pulled from a larger spell.

“This was tied to the left shoe,” he said. “When it was cut, I felt it.”

Mara stared at the lace. “You felt it?”

Anansi gave her a look that suggested she was lagging behind on purpose. “Yes.”

“Like pain?”

He hesitated. For the first time since entering the shop, he looked, if not vulnerable, then at least less certain.

“Like being late to one’s own name,” he said.

The sentence was so strange and so unexpectedly sad that Mara did not know what to do with it.

Kofi reached for the lace, stopped, then withdrew his hand. “Who would cut it?”

Anansi’s face hardened. “Someone who remembers the old rules. Someone who thinks motion should belong only to those who can afford to control it.”

Mara opened her mouth, then shut it again. There was too much in that sentence to unpack in one go. People who controlled motion were called different things in different neighborhoods. Employers. Landlords. Police. Gods.

She looked around Kofi’s small shop, at the shoes lined in rows, each one a small economy of repair. She thought of the city outside—its routes, its escalators, its lanes, its locked doors. She thought of her own feet, her own job, her own endless day of carrying other people’s things between places.

“Suppose we help you,” she said. “What happens after?”

Anansi met her eyes.

“I get the shoes back,” he said. “And then I stop the path from tearing wider.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“No,” he said softly. “It isn’t.”

And for the first time, Mara thought she heard something like fear under the smoothness of his voice.

Not fear of dying. Something older than that. Fear of becoming irrelevant. Fear of being unable to move where movement mattered.

She hated that she understood it.

Outside, thunder muttered again. Inside, the damaged black shoes sat on the bench like a challenge no one had properly named yet.

Kofi broke the silence first.

“If we’re doing this,” he said, “I want to know where to start.”

Anansi’s expression sharpened into approval, or relief, or the nearest thing gods had to either.

“At the place where lost things are handed off,” he said. “The station beneath the market.”

Mara looked at the door.

Then at her broken sneaker.

Then at the god who wore white shoes like a warning.

“Fine,” she said. “But if this turns into some kind of prophecy, I’m leaving.”

Anansi smiled.

“It already has.”
step_outputs.8:
The station beneath the market had been closed for eleven years and used for three different things since.

First it had become a storage space for the market stalls above, where broken umbrellas, cracked crates, and surplus plastic chairs went to gather dust in pale piles. Then someone had decided the tiled tunnel made a convenient place for illegal cable runs, and for a while it hummed at night with stolen electricity. Now it belonged mostly to the pigeons and to the people who knew not to ask who else was using it.

Mara knew the entrance because the lock on the service gate had been bent open long ago and never properly repaired. Kofi knew it because he knew the city in the way some people knew family gossip: not every detail, but enough to understand the pattern of where people hid their bad decisions.

Anansi knew it because, he said, “all roads remember themselves if you give them time.”

He had laughed when Mara repeated that aloud.

The three of them stood just inside the service stairwell while market noise rattled faintly through the concrete above. Water dripped somewhere in the dark. The air smelled of rust, old wet plaster, and fish from the stalls overhead.

Mara had a flashlight in one hand and her courier bag still over one shoulder because she had not had time to stop being herself before being recruited into myth.

Kofi held a small tool roll under his arm. He had not explained why. He had simply said, “If we are going below, I’m not going empty-handed.”

Anansi, of course, had come carrying nothing.

“You could have brought a light,” Mara said.

“I did.”

“You mean your personality?”

He smiled. “Exactly.”

Kofi muttered, “If this gets us killed, I’ll be very annoyed.”

“That’s the spirit,” Anansi said.

They descended the stairs. Halfway down, the city sounds above them became muffled and then almost gone, replaced by the damp silence of a place that had once been built for crowds and now waited, empty and listening, for some other arrival.

At the bottom, the station opened in front of them like the memory of a throat.

Old tiled walls, once white, now stained with years of seepage and grime. Tracks buried under a layer of grit and debris. A yellow line on the platform edge faded almost to nothing. Overhead signs still hung from rusted brackets, the letters erased by time and vandalism so thoroughly that only fragments remained: EXIT, PLATFORM, LINE 4. A schedule board no longer used had been covered with stickers and tag paint and, in one corner, a small pasted image of a sneaker with wings drawn on it in red marker.

Mara stared at that.

Anansi noticed. “Someone has been here.”

“Obviously,” she said. “The pigeon population alone suggests it.”

He gave her a sidelong look. “Not that someone.”

Kofi crouched to examine the floor near the platform edge. “These marks are fresh.”

Mara shone her light down. Faint drag lines crossed the dust, too broad for a boot sole, too even for a crate. Something had been moved here recently. Something heavy. Or something carried by many hands.

Then she saw the scuffs.

Shoe prints.

Not a clear trail, only impressions left in wet dust and then partly smeared. But they were there. Some narrow. Some wide. Some with the telltale asymmetry of a person whose heel had worn down on one side. And among them, one print was different: deeper, cleaner, almost luminous at the edges, as if the floor itself had hesitated around it.

Mara knelt before she could stop herself.

“These are all from different shoes,” she said.

Kofi came to stand beside her. “Yes.”

“How can you tell?”

He pointed with one finger. “This one’s cheap rubber. This one’s been resoled. This one’s from a tread I haven’t seen in twenty years.”

Mara looked up at him. “You can do that by looking at mud?”

“Don’t sound so surprised. It’s my trade.”

Anansi had wandered a few paces ahead, hands in his coat pockets, studying the tiled wall. “There’s a handoff point here.”

“A what?” Mara said.

“Lost things are passed through places like this. Not always deliberately. Sometimes a bad decision needs a corridor.”

Kofi snorted. “That sentence should be illegal.”

Anansi ignored him.

Mara shone her light toward the far end of the platform. A tunnel mouth yawned there, black and damp and half-filled with old plastic sheeting that had torn into strips. Something stirred in the darkness beyond, and she tightened her grip on the flashlight.

“Do you hear that?” she asked.

Kofi listened. “Water.”

Anansi’s head tilted. “No.”

Something clicked softly in the dark.

Then another sound. A shuffle. Not from one body, but many.

Mara’s skin tightened along her arms. The flashlight beam wavered. “Tell me that’s a rat problem.”

Anansi’s voice changed, just a little. Sharper. “Stay on the platform.”

From the tunnel mouth, figures stepped into the light.

At first Mara thought they were people. Then she saw how wrong the movement was. Their limbs moved with the uncertain coordination of sleepwalkers. Their heads were lowered. Their clothes were damp and dark with tunnel water. Each of them wore shoes.

Not matching ones. Not even pairs. One had a wedding shoe and a sneaker. Another wore a single red heel and a child’s sandal. A man in a blazer wore running shoes with one lace missing. A woman in a hospital gown had walking boots on feet that did not seem to belong to her. Their faces were blank with the focus of people following instructions they no longer remembered.

They did not look at Mara, Kofi, or Anansi.

They looked at the ground between them.

At the light around Anansi’s feet.

“Don’t let them touch me,” he said, and for once there was no playfulness in his voice.

The figures began to move faster.

Mara backed up instinctively. “What are they?”

“Borrowers,” said Kofi under his breath.

Anansi snapped his head toward him. “You know them?”

“I know a type.”

The first figure stepped onto the platform. Its shoes made no sound. Another followed. Then another. The air in the station shifted, as if the empty space itself had begun to fill with pressure.

Mara trained the flashlight on their faces and saw nothing but exhaustion and glassiness, as if each person had been walked empty. In the center of the group, something bright flashed at the back of one throat—a glint of metal, maybe, or a reflection. Then it was gone.

The woman in the hospital gown lifted her head.

Her eyes were open, but not awake.

She looked directly at Mara and said, in a voice that did not belong to the body speaking it, “Return what was taken.”

Then she smiled, and the smile was wrong enough to make Mara step back hard against the wall.

Anansi hissed, “No.”

The figures surged.

Kofi grabbed Mara by the shoulder and shoved her sideways just as the first borrower lunged. Its hand skidded across the tiles where her coat had been. Anansi moved with sudden violence, one arm outstretched, and the air in front of him seemed to buckle. The nearest borrower stumbled as if it had hit a wall.

Mara’s heartbeat punched loud in her ears.

“Run?” she shouted.

“Not yet!” Anansi snapped. “If they get the shoes—”

“I’m aware that’s bad!”

Another figure came around from the left, dragging one foot. Kofi swung his tool roll with surprising force and hit it square in the shin. The figure folded with a wet, startled gasp, then got back up as if pain was only an inconvenience.

Mara saw something then, in the spill of her flashlight: one of the borrower’s shoes had a cut lace tied through the eyelet like a leash. The knot was bright white.

Not the lace from Anansi’s coat pocket. Another one. But the same kind.

“These are connected,” she shouted.

Anansi looked at her sharply. “Yes.”

“Connected to what?”

“To the pair you saw.”

Another borrower reached the platform edge and crouched, fingers spreading over the tiles as though feeling for a seam. The glint at its throat flashed again.

Mara lunged forward before she had time to think about it. She caught the flashlight in one hand and shone it directly into the borrower’s face. It recoiled, blinking hard. The movement was small but real. Human.

That startled her more than the rest of it.

“Kofi!” she yelled. “What do I do?”

He was already opening his tool roll. “Anything that breaks the pattern!”

“Very helpful!”

He threw her a strip of waxed thread. “Tie something!”

She caught it on reflex.

Anansi barked, “Do not let them complete the handoff!”

“Great,” Mara said, because that was apparently all the instruction anyone was going to get. “Wonderful. Love this.”

She looked around wildly. A discarded maintenance cart stood half-hidden near the tunnel wall. On it sat a coil of old cable, a rusted wrench, and a broken plastic chair. Nothing useful. Nothing except, on the lower shelf, a box of mismatched laces in a dozen colors, all tangled together.

Mara snatched the box and flung it across the platform.

The laces burst open in the air like spilled veins of color. For a fraction of a second the borrowers all turned toward them, their attention snagged by the movement. One reached instinctively, then stopped, confused. Another bent to pick one up and stared at it with a hunger so blank and so lonely that Mara felt something cold in her chest.

Then the far end of the tunnel darkened.

Not darkened—tightened.

As if something large had just stepped to the other side of the station.

The borrowers froze.

Anansi went very still.

Kofi whispered, “What now?”

From the tunnel mouth, a pair of white sneakers emerged.

Not Anansi’s. These were older, their canvas yellowed, the soles nicked and repaired in three different places. The laces were gone. Around them, the air seemed to ripple with heat. Then a voice came from the dark behind them, low and steady.

“Leave them,” it said.

The borrowers obeyed at once, heads dropping, bodies retreating as though pulled by invisible cords.

Mara swallowed.

Because she knew that voice, even though she had heard it only once before.

It was the man from the awning.

Only now he was standing in the tunnel mouth as if he had always been there.

And on his feet, like a theft made visible, were the missing shoes.
step_outputs.9:
The man in the tunnel had the kind of face that made it difficult to tell whether you were looking at a person or at an idea that had learned to wear a person briefly.

Up close, Mara could see that his coat had a fine layer of dust across the shoulders, as if he had come from somewhere that still had wind in it. His eyes were dark and level and older than his hands. The white sneakers on his feet looked wrong in a new way now that she knew they were the missing pair: not merely out of place, but absent from the order of things. They seemed to belong to no shelf, no store, no ordinary history of wear.

The borrowers had gone still in the tunnel behind him, crouched and waiting like people who had forgotten their own names.

Anansi took one step forward, then stopped.

“You’re bold,” he said.

The man tilted his head. “You say that as if boldness is unusual for gods.”

Kofi exhaled through his nose. “So there it is.”

Mara stared from one to the other. “You know him.”

Anansi’s expression was unreadable. “Yes.”

The man smiled faintly. “I’m hurt that you sound so unenthusiastic, old friend.”

“Ekwu,” Anansi said.

The name landed in the station with the weight of a door shutting. Even the borrowers seemed to react, their shoulders tightening a fraction.

Mara looked at Ekwu. “You’re the one who took the shoes.”

“I reclaimed what was taken from me.”

Anansi’s eyes hardened. “No, you stole a threshold and tied it to frightened people.”

Ekwu glanced down at the sneakers on his feet with an expression that was almost disdain. “You wear your old tricks as if they were innocence. The road cannot belong to you forever.”

“It doesn’t belong to me.”

“It does when you use it to make the world forget where it stands.”

Mara felt Kofi shift beside her. He was listening the way he listened to shoes: not to the words alone, but to the wear beneath them.

Ekwu turned to Mara, and something in his gaze sharpened with interest. “You are the one who sees before understanding. That is useful, if undereducated.”

“Thanks,” Mara said flatly. “I’ll treasure that.”

He ignored the tone. “These shoes carry passage. Passage makes people careless. They think a threshold is neutral. They think a door is only a convenience between one place and another. But a threshold is where power gathers. It is where a thing becomes vulnerable.”

Anansi gave a dry laugh. “Listen to him. He sounds almost charitable when he’s angry.”

Ekwu’s face did not move. “I am not angry.”

“You’re wearing stolen shoes.”

“I’m wearing the only form of correction you understand.”

Mara looked at the pair on his feet. From this distance she could see that the right sole had been restitched, and not by a craftsman who expected the work to hold for long. Whoever repaired them had done it in haste, with rough thread and too much tension. The shoe looked strained, as if it were resisting the body inside it.

“Why take them?” she asked. “If they’re important, why not just ask for them?”

Ekwu regarded her for a long moment, as if deciding whether her question had been naive or merely human.

“Because asking,” he said, “suggests equality.”

Anansi snorted softly. “There he is.”

Ekwu did not glance at him. “These shoes were made for crossing. For entering, leaving, returning. The modern world believes crossing is freedom. The old world knew crossing was a privilege earned by cost. The more you move without paying attention, the thinner the boundary grows. The roads become hungry.”

Mara looked at the borrowers. Their blank faces, their mismatched shoes, the leash-like white laces attached to some unseen point of command. She felt a disgust she could not entirely name.

“You did this to them,” she said.

“I opened them to use.”

“Same thing,” she said.

The faintest tension appeared at the corners of Ekwu’s mouth. “You think morality is simple because you have not yet been asked to carry anything sacred.”

Kofi spoke for the first time in several minutes. “It looks to me like you’ve asked the wrong people to carry it.”

Ekwu’s gaze shifted to him. “And yet here you are.”

Kofi’s hands flexed once at his sides. “Only because your shoes are badly made.”

For a moment Mara thought Ekwu might be offended enough to strike him. Instead, to her surprise, the god looked almost amused.

“They hold,” he said.

“For now,” Kofi replied.

Anansi moved his weight from one foot to the other, impatience tightening the air around him. “You can lecture us from your throne later. Where did you get the borrowers?”

Ekwu smiled without warmth. “Borrowed them.”

“That’s not funny.”

“It wasn’t meant to be.”

He shifted his stance, and Mara saw then that the shoes were not sitting comfortably on him. They clung to his feet like an argument. The laces were threaded too tightly. The tongue of the left shoe had folded under in a way that must have pinched.

Ekwu noticed her looking and his expression cooled.

“You understand now,” he said. “You saw me because the shoes were already calling for repair. The pair you found in the shop were not merely damaged. They were failing.”

Anansi’s face changed. “You forced the crossing.”

“I stabilized it.”

“You ripped it.”

“I prevented collapse.”

Mara looked between them. Their anger felt older than the station, older than the city. Not sibling anger, exactly. Something more like theological resentment. Two different ideas of what should survive.

She said, “What happens when the shoes fail?”

Anansi answered without looking at her. “The threshold opens wrong.”

Ekwu said at the same time, “The threshold stops serving.”

Mara rubbed her forehead. “Those are not the same answer.”

“No,” Kofi said quietly, “but they’re both bad.”

The borrowers remained motionless behind Ekwu, eyes lowered. One of them had begun to cry, but without sound, tears slipping down over an expression that did not know what to do with grief.

Mara saw the glint again at the throat of the hospital-gown woman—a tiny metal tag, maybe. No, not a tag. A key.

She frowned. “What’s that?”

Ekwu’s eyes shifted to where she pointed, and for the first time a crack appeared in his composure.

Kofi saw it too. “That’s not part of the shoes.”

“Of course it is,” Ekwu said.

Anansi’s voice went flat. “No. You’ve used a key.”

Ekwu did not answer.

Mara looked from one god to the other, the pieces rearranging themselves in her head without fitting cleanly. “Used it for what?”

Anansi’s expression darkened with understanding. “He’s not just keeping the path from tearing wider.”

Ekwu said nothing.

Mara felt the room tilt very slightly around that silence.

Anansi continued, his voice quieter now, stripped of all teasing. “He’s trying to reopen an old route.”

Ekwu’s face remained composed, but the silence was confirmation enough.

Mara stared at him. “To where?”

Ekwu looked past her, as if the answer was too large to fit in the tunnel.

“The places mortals stopped going,” he said.

Kofi went very still.

Anansi’s jaw tightened. “You cannot mean—”

“I mean exactly what I mean.”

“No,” Anansi said. “You’re not that foolish.”

Ekwu’s voice sharpened. “And you are not that wise.”

Mara looked at the white sneakers on Ekwu’s feet, the split seam, the tied thread, the key hanging against a throat that did not need breath. Suddenly the shoes did not seem like stolen objects at all. They looked like a bridge under strain. Like a body holding up more than it should.

She understood enough to be afraid, and not enough to know what kind of afraid.

“The shoes are a gate,” she said.

Ekwu looked at her with something like approval. “A gate requires a keeper.”

“Then why not keep it with your own feet?”

His face changed then, just barely, and she saw the answer before he gave it.

Because he could not walk the route alone.

Because no god could.

Because the shoes were not just power but permission, and the permission had to come from somewhere older than pride.

Anansi exhaled sharply, as if the truth had just struck him in the ribs. “You used the borrowers to test the crossing.”

Ekwu did not deny it.

“They are empty enough to carry the strain,” he said. “Most mortals would have broken.”

Mara’s stomach turned. “You used people like that?”

“People are always used by larger things,” Ekwu said. “At least this way they were useful to the design.”

“That,” Mara said, voice suddenly very steady, “is the worst thing you’ve said so far.”

A strange thing happened then.

Ekwu looked at her as if he had not expected to be understood so accurately by someone he had dismissed five minutes earlier.

For a heartbeat, no one spoke.

Then Anansi said, very softly, “How long have you been trying to open it?”

Ekwu did not answer.

That was answer enough.

Mara looked at the station walls, the faded signs, the old tracks buried under grit. She thought of all the places people stopped going and then stopped remembering. Stations. Temples. Back rooms. Borders. The routes between places that only mattered until they didn’t.

And then she thought of her own life, how often she had been crossing things without noticing where she stood.

Kofi broke the silence with a practical question. “If the route reopens, what comes through?”

Ekwu’s gaze remained fixed ahead. “What was left behind.”

The words landed cold and heavy.

Mara looked at the borrowers again. She did not know what they had lost to become this, but she knew enough to understand that people did not become empty by accident.

Anansi took a step back, the first clear retreat Mara had seen from him. “You have no idea what you’re doing.”

Ekwu’s expression finally sharpened into something dangerous. “I know exactly what I’m doing.”

“No,” said Anansi. “You know what you want.”

Ekwu’s shoes shifted on the tile, and Mara heard the small, ugly sound of strain in the stitched seam. The left sneaker was beginning to fail again.

She saw it at the same moment the god did.

For the first time, genuine alarm crossed Ekwu’s face.

And Mara understood, with a sudden strange clarity, that the missing thing was not only the shoes. It was the reason anyone had ever trusted them to hold.

She said, before she could stop herself, “Kofi—”

But before she could finish, the seam on Ekwu’s left shoe split open with a sharp crack like a snapped bone, and the whole station dropped half a degree into darkness.
step_outputs.10:
The sound of the seam splitting did not echo.

It swallowed.

For a moment the station seemed to inhale everything—light, air, breath, the faint drip from the ceiling—and hold it all at the center of the crack in Ekwu’s shoe. Mara felt the hairs on her arms rise. The borrowers behind him gave a collective shudder, like puppets with their strings tugged hard.

Then the darkness thinned again, and everybody was still where they had been, except nothing about the platform felt stable anymore.

Ekwu looked down at his left foot.

The shoe had opened along the inner seam, the white thread torn clean through. Beneath it was not sock, not skin, but a flicker of blackness that made Mara think of deep water at night. It vanished as soon as she focused on it.

Anansi swore under his breath.

Kofi said, “I told you.”

No one answered him.

Ekwu’s face had gone completely still. Not calm—worse than calm. Focused with panic hidden so deep it had become precision.

“Now,” Anansi said, “we leave.”

Ekwu’s eyes lifted. “No.”

“That was not a suggestion.”

Mara backed toward the stairwell instinctively, but the borrowers were moving again. Not forward this time—backward, in a slow, disorderly drift, as if the opening seam had loosened the knot of whatever held them in place. One of them turned its head and looked at her with startled human fear.

Mara stopped.

“Are they waking up?” she asked.

Kofi answered first. “No. They’re being released.”

“By what?”

“The shoes,” said Anansi.

Ekwu snapped, “Enough.”

The word hit the platform like a command issued to the bones of the building. For one breath the borrowers froze.

Then, unexpectedly, Mara saw fear in Ekwu’s face too. Not for himself. For what was coming through the split.

The tunnel mouth behind him darkened again.

Something moved there.

Not a person. Not yet. A shape, maybe, too large to fit cleanly into the opening. The borrowed bodies on the platform began to tremble. One woman dropped to her knees and gripped her own shoes like she was trying to hold herself together.

Kofi stepped closer to Mara. “We need light.”

Mara raised the flashlight and aimed it into the tunnel. The beam touched the darkness and seemed to bend.

Anansi moved at once, striding toward the platform edge. “If you’re still planning to force the route—”

“I said no,” Ekwu replied.

“But you’re not leaving.”

Ekwu did not deny that either.

A pulse moved through the station floor, something between a tremor and a heartbeat. Dust lifted from the track bed in a thin gray wave. Mara heard, faintly, the sound of shoes hitting pavement somewhere far below, or above, or on the other side of the station entirely.

Then the first of the borrowers screamed.

The scream came from a man in a blazer with one running shoe and one polished dress shoe. It was a raw, human sound of sudden awareness. He clutched at his head as if trying to keep his thoughts from spilling out. Another borrower stumbled and stared at her hands in horror, as though discovering them for the first time.

“Something’s inside them,” Mara said.

Anansi’s face tightened. “Not something. A route.”

Kofi looked at him sharply. “Explain.”

Anansi did not take his eyes off the tunnel. “The shoes were made to carry passage without letting passage take root. Ekwu has threaded the wrong direction into the soles.”

Mara frowned, trying to keep up. “Meaning?”

“Meaning,” Kofi said grimly, “he turned them into a lever.”

Ekwu spun on him. “They were already failing.”

“You made them fail harder.”

“To what end?” Mara asked.

Neither god answered.

That silence was enough. Mara looked from one to the other and saw, with a sinking feeling, that this was not just a stolen-shoe problem. This had been going on long before today. Long before her. Long before the station. They had fought over this route before, or over what should be allowed to cross it, and now the argument had become physical enough to tear human bodies open around the edges.

The tunnel shape shifted.

Something stepped closer.

Mara could not see it clearly. Only hints: a shoulder too broad, a hand that seemed made of shadow and wet shine, the suggestion of a face in negative space. It remained just beyond the beam of the flashlight, which seemed to shudder whenever she tried to hold it steady.

One of the borrowers began to sing.

Not a real song. A broken line of sound, half remembered, half heard through years of use. It made Mara’s stomach clench because it sounded like the kind of thing people sang when crossing into places they hoped not to see.

Kofi reached into his tool roll and pulled out a small awl and a spool of thick thread.

Mara stared at him. “You brought shoemaking tools to a supernatural collapse?”

He glanced at her. “You preferred I came unprepared?”

Fair point. She hated that.

Anansi’s gaze flicked to the tools. “Can you repair the seam?”

“Not with whatever damage you’ve made.”

“Try.”

Kofi barked a humorless laugh. “That’s your strategy? Try?”

“It’s usually worked better than surrender.”

Mara looked at Ekwu. “Will fixing the shoe stop it?”

Ekwu’s answer came after the smallest pause. “It will slow the opening.”

“That sounds like not enough.”

“It may be all that is possible.”

Anansi’s mouth flattened. “No. There’s another way.”

Ekwu’s eyes flashed. “There is not.”

“Yes,” Anansi said. “There is. You give up the key.”

Ekwu’s whole body stilled.

Mara looked between them. “What key?”

Anansi pointed toward the thing hanging at Ekwu’s throat. A small metal object, dark with age and so worn it almost blended into the fabric beneath it.

Ekwu’s hand rose instinctively to cover it.

“That,” Anansi said, “opens the old route. The one you’ve been trying to reach through the shoes. Give it up, and the shoes become only shoes again.”

Ekwu’s expression became almost cruel. “And lose the way back?”

“It was never yours alone.”

The tunnels groaned.

Not a sound from stone, but from something beneath stone, something old and unwilling. The platform lights flickered. The borrowers cried out as the pressure changed around them. Mara felt it in her own teeth.

Ekwu’s gaze moved to the failing shoe. “If I remove the key, the path closes.”

“Good,” said Anansi.

Ekwu looked at him with open contempt. “You think that is victory.”

“I think it’s less catastrophic.”

“I think you fear what might return.”

Anansi’s expression shuttered.

Mara noticed that, and noticed too that Kofi had gone very quiet. He was staring not at the gods but at the borrowers, as if he had already made up his mind about the only thing in the room he could fix.

One of the borrowers—a young woman with a school backpack and one red sneaker—stumbled into the flashlight beam and whispered, “Please.”

The word was so ordinary that Mara felt it like a bruise.

Please.

Not from the gods. From a person inside the mess.

Mara took a step forward. “Can you tell them apart from whatever’s in here?”

Anansi looked at her, surprised by the question. “At the edge? Sometimes.”

“Then do that.”

He frowned. “What?”

“Help me get the people out.”

Kofi swore softly. “Mara—”

“No,” she said, without taking her eyes off the borrowers. “If we’re choosing between letting the station open and letting people get swallowed by it, I know which one I’m choosing.”

Ekwu’s face tightened at her tone. He had not expected a mortal to speak like a judge.

“Foolish,” he said.

Mara looked at him. “Probably.”

Then she turned to Kofi. “How do we get them moving?”

He glanced once at the spread of mismatched laces on the floor from earlier. His eyes narrowed. “Pattern disruption,” he said.

“English.”

“Anything that reminds them they’re separate from the route.”

Anansi caught on immediately. “Noise. Change. Interruptions.”

Mara stared. “That is still not a plan.”

“It is now,” said Kofi.

He grabbed the nearest loose shoelace from his tool roll and snapped it between his hands like a signal. Then he began tying knots at speed—too fast for ordinary craft, precise enough that Mara could see he was not simply making knots but setting a rhythm. A pattern. A refusal.

Anansi moved at once, sweeping his hand through the air. The flashlight beam fractured into several smaller beams, each caught on a different borrower’s face. In the sudden scatter of light, the figures jerked and blinked as if waking from a long spell.

Mara understood then, abruptly, what her part was.

She ran.

Not away. Along the platform, toward the borrowers, toward the place where the route seemed thickest. She shouted names she did not know, questions, nonsense—anything human and random. “Hey! Your shoe’s untied! No, the other one! Don’t look at me like that, I’m trying to help—”

One borrower turned her head at the sound of the voice, not the words, and for an instant Mara saw a person in there: frightened, exhausted, confused. Enough.

“Kofi!” she yelled, “Now!”

He threw her a length of thick thread. She caught it one-handed, nearly slipping on the grit, and tied it around the metal railing at the platform edge, looping it through her fist as she ran. It was ridiculous. It was maybe nothing. But the thread bit into her palm and made the motion her own.

Anansi appeared at her shoulder. “That won’t hold a god.”

“I’m not trying to hold a god.”

She yanked the thread hard, snapping it against the railing with a sharp twang.

The sound cut through the station like a bell.

Several borrowers flinched. One dropped to the floor, gasping as if the noise had found a trapped place in her lungs and opened it.

Ekwu looked up, startled.

The key at his throat shifted.

Mara saw her chance and did not think about it.

She lunged.

Her fingers closed around the chain just as Ekwu’s hand came up. The metal was cold enough to sting. He caught her wrist with impossible force, and for one breath they stood locked together—mortal and god, both refusing to yield.

His eyes met hers.

“Let go,” he said.

“No.”

Then Kofi’s voice rang out, sharp as a tool striking steel. “Mara!”

She did not know what he was warning her about until the tunnel behind Ekwu convulsed.

The dark shape at the mouth of it had reached the split seam in the shoe. The light around it bent inward. The borrowers screamed. Ekwu’s grip on her wrist tightened, and the key flashed once at his throat—

Then snapped free.

Mara tore backward, nearly falling as the chain broke in her hand.

The key spun through the air, a small dark arc, and dropped into Kofi’s open palm.

The station went silent.

Not calm. Silent in the way a body goes silent just before it remembers pain.

Ekwu stared at his empty throat.

Then at Kofi.

Then at Mara.

The failing shoe at his foot emitted a sound like thread tearing underwater.

And the route behind him began to open.
step_outputs.11:
Kofi had never liked being the center of a supernatural crisis.

In the ordinary world, being noticed usually meant somebody wanted something fixed, polished, or argued over. In the station beneath the market, it meant a dead thing reaching for his hand.

The key was colder than he expected. Not metal-cold. Worse. It felt like holding a memory that did not belong to him. Even through the strain of the noise and the shaking platform, he was aware of how wrong it was to have it, how quickly the space around him seemed to recognize the theft.

Mara was still crouched by the railing, breathing hard, one hand around her wrist where Ekwu had grabbed her. Anansi stood a few paces away, his face tightened into something Kofi had never seen on him before. Not anger. Calculation edged with alarm.

Ekwu had gone utterly still.

The opening in his left shoe had widened to a slit. From inside it, the darkness was no longer darkness but depth, and depth was beginning to spill. The borrowers were stumbling backward in uneven panic, some crying, some laughing in shock, one man clawing at his own shirt as if trying to tear himself out of it.

Mara looked up. “Kofi—what do we do?”

He did not answer immediately because he could see the key changing in his hand. The ridges along its shaft were moving, or maybe his eye was too afraid to settle on one shape. Small lines appeared in the metal, patterns like overlapping roads.

Anansi saw it too. “Do not let it touch the floor.”

“Why?” Kofi snapped.

“Because it remembers where it came from.”

“That is not helping.”

“No,” Anansi said, “but it is true.”

The station lights flickered violently. One overhead bulb burst. Glass rained in a glittering spill down the platform. The borrowers flinched again, and that flinch seemed to loosen the thing holding them. A woman in a hospital gown looked at her own hands and started sobbing with sudden, terrible recognition.

Mara stood. “They’re waking up.”

“Some of them,” said Anansi.

“Can we get them out?”

“Before the route fully opens? Maybe.”

“Then maybe is enough.”

Kofi looked at her sharply. That was the kind of thing she said when she had already decided not to leave people behind, no matter how poor the odds.

Ekwu’s voice cut through the station, low and furious. “You have no idea what you have done.”

Mara turned toward him. “You first used the people.”

“I used them to keep the path from tearing apart.”

“You cut it open.”

“I strengthened it.”

“By stuffing frightened bodies into it?”

Ekwu’s face flashed with contempt and something more dangerous beneath it. “You speak as if pain is a moral category.”

“It is when you make it someone else’s problem,” Mara said.

For a second Kofi thought Ekwu would strike her. Instead he laughed once, sharply, with no humor in it at all.

“You think this is about cruelty,” he said. “No. It is about forgetting. Your world has become so obsessed with movement that it no longer understands the cost of arrival.”

Anansi’s expression darkened. “Save your sermon.”

Ekwu ignored him. “This route once mattered. It led to places mortals named only in fear. It held memory. It held obligations. Then the roads changed. The stations closed. The offerings stopped. You all walked elsewhere and called it progress.”

Kofi tightened his hand around the key. “And so you stole bodies.”

Ekwu’s gaze snapped to him. “I borrowed what was already being wasted.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer you’re getting.”

The route behind him pulsed.

Kofi felt it in the bones of his wrist. The key in his hand was tugging now, not physically but by direction, as if part of it wanted to be back where it belonged. He clenched harder.

Anansi stepped closer to the platform edge and looked into the opening in the shoe. His face had gone hard. “You did not just want to reopen the old crossing.”

Ekwu said nothing.

Anansi’s voice sharpened. “You wanted to bring something through it.”

The silence that followed was answer enough.

Mara saw it too, and her face changed. “What?”

Ekwu’s expression did not move.

Anansi said, with sudden quiet disbelief, “You don’t know what you’ve invited.”

“I know more than you think.”

“No,” Anansi said. “You know the shape of your regret and have mistaken it for wisdom.”

That landed.

Even Kofi felt it.

Ekwu’s jaw tightened. “There are things that should not have been abandoned.”

“Abandoned?” Mara repeated. “You mean trapped.”

The route opened a little more. Darkness pushed against the shoe seam. The canvas buckled around the split, holding just barely.

One of the borrowers screamed as a memory hit her all at once. She fell to her knees, clutching at her head, and Kofi saw a tiny metal tag flash at the edge of her collar. Not a tag. Another key, smaller than Ekwu’s, worked through a chain by the look of it. Maybe all of them had one. Maybe the route had been seeded into them like splinters.

He didn’t have time to think on that.

Mara was already moving toward the borrowers, lifting her voice, trying to keep them oriented.

“Listen to me,” she said. “Everyone look at me. If you can hear me, move away from the tunnel. Don’t run at once—just move. Follow the light.”

A young man in mismatched shoes stared at her with tears in his eyes and then, shockingly, nodded.

Kofi had the sudden, absurd urge to laugh. Not because anything was funny, but because she had become, in less than an hour, the sort of person people listened to in disasters. He saw in her the exact thing gods always seemed to miss: people in panic needed direction, yes, but they needed it from someone who looked like she also had a reason not to be crushed.

He looked at the key again.

Patterned, warm now, and still tugging.

Anansi watched him. “If you can feel it, you can use it.”

Kofi barked a laugh. “Use a cursed key to fix a divine breach. That seems wise.”

“It’s not cursed,” Anansi said. “It’s attached.”

“To what?”

Anansi’s gaze flicked toward Ekwu, then to the widening seam. “To the pair. To the opening. To what he’s been trying to return.”

Mara heard that and turned, her eyes widening slightly. “Return?”

Ekwu’s face went unreadable again. But too late. The word had already exposed him.

Kofi said slowly, “You’re not trying to let something out.”

Ekwu did not answer.

“You’re trying to get something back.”

The god’s silence was long enough to be painful.

Then, with a kind of bitter pride, Ekwu said, “There are doors that should not remain shut forever.”

Anansi closed his eyes for one brief, disgusted moment. “Oh, you fool.”

Mara stared. “What is he talking about?”

Kofi looked at the route, at the dark seam, at the pressure behind it. Something was now distinctly pressing from the other side, not bursting through but reaching, testing, as if feeling for the shape of a world that had changed while it slept.

He thought of old stations, closed tunnels, shut gates. Of things left behind because no one knew how to carry them. Or because carrying them had become inconvenient.

Not all absence was mercy.

Not all return was rescue.

He hated that answer because it was true.

Mara was still moving the borrowers back, one by one, speaking to them as if they were simply exhausted and not half unmade by divine infrastructure. A woman in a red coat clutched Mara’s sleeve and wept silently. Mara steadied her without hesitation. No ceremony. Just hands.

Anansi looked from Mara to Kofi and said, quietly, “If he gets the route open fully, it won’t stay in the station.”

Kofi knew that much from the way the air had changed. The pressure was spreading.

“What do you want me to do?”

Anansi pointed at the key.

Kofi looked down at it. “You want me to use this?”

“I want you to stop holding it like an answer and start holding it like a lever.”

“That is not reassuring.”

“I’m aware.”

Ekwu’s lips parted slightly. For the first time, his composure cracked in visible strain. “Do not.”

The word landed on all of them.

Kofi realized then that the key was not only opening the route. It was holding him, too. Its pull was directional, but not toward the opening. Toward the shoes. Toward the seam. Toward the old path beneath the new city.

He could feel it in his arm now, a tug like a rope drawn taut through his bones.

“What happens if I turn it?” he asked.

Anansi answered carefully. “The route shifts.”

“Toward where?”

“Somewhere it was meant to go.”

Ekwu said, “You have no idea what you are asking.”

Kofi looked at him. “For once, I think I do.”

The god’s eyes narrowed.

Kofi understood, then, something ugly and simple: Ekwu had not merely been trying to bring something through. He had been trying to force the city to remember a path it had abandoned. The old crossing was not a metaphor to him. It was a grievance. A correction. A place where the forgotten could insist on being known.

And maybe that was noble, once. Maybe. But he had chosen the wrong bodies, the wrong shoes, the wrong moment, and now the correction was becoming a disaster.

Mara came back to the platform edge, breathing hard. “Most of them are moving.”

“Good,” said Anansi. “Keep them moving.”

She looked at Kofi, then at the key in his fist. “Can you fix it?”

Kofi almost said no out of habit.

Instead he looked at the torn seam in Ekwu’s shoe.

At the stitching. At the strain. At the fact that the shoe was trying, in its own way, to remain a shoe while also being a gate.

He took a breath.

Then he said, “Not by mending alone.”

Mara nodded once, as if that was all she needed.

That trust hit harder than the crisis.

Kofi stepped toward the platform edge.

Anansi moved with him. “If you turn that key, I don’t know what comes.”

Kofi glanced at him. “That makes two of us.”

And then, because there was nothing else for it, he lowered the key toward the torn shoe and turned it.

The station groaned.

Not with sound but with recognition.

The split seam flashed white. The borrowers cried out. The air rushed backward with such force Mara staggered and grabbed the railing. Anansi threw out one hand to steady the nearest collapsing body. Ekwu’s face went white with fury and something like grief.

And from the opened route came a smell Kofi would later struggle to name: rain on stone, old incense, dust long sealed away, and something else, something like a room full of people who had been waiting centuries to be let in.

The darkness on the other side shifted.

And stepped closer.
step_outputs.12:
The thing at the other side of the opening did not come through all at once.

At first it was only pressure, a shape suggested by the way the air folded around it. Then a hand appeared—if it was a hand—long-fingered, gray with dust, one knuckle bent at an angle that made Kofi’s stomach turn. The borrowers cried out and pressed backward along the platform, but Mara was already moving among them, pushing shoulders, guiding elbows, telling them to keep going toward the stairs.

“Up,” she shouted. “Keep moving up. Don’t look at it. Just keep moving.”

Her voice was hoarse now, but it held. People listened.

Kofi stood with the key half-turned in his fist, every muscle in his arm quivering with the effort of holding it against the pull. The route beneath Ekwu’s split shoe had become a wound in the station floor. Light, if it could be called that, seeped out of it in thin pale threads.

Anansi had planted himself between the opening and the retreating borrowers. His hands moved in quick, sharp gestures, and each one seemed to place a momentary knot in the air. The shape at the threshold hit one of those knots and slowed, not stopped, but enough for its outline to sharpen.

It was a person.

Or something that had once been one.

Kofi saw a face. Not clearly. A suggestion of features crowded into a surface too long exposed to weather. Eyes like wet stone. A mouth that had forgotten how to close properly. It wore no shoes.

It stepped forward another inch and the station lights all dimmed at once.

Ekwu made a sound then—small, involuntary, nothing like the god he had been pretending to be. Not fear. Recognition.

“No,” he said.

Anansi turned on him, fury finally breaking loose. “You absolute fool.”

Ekwu’s gaze was fixed on the figure in the opening. “I did not think it would be this far.”

Mara, hauling a terrified borrower by the sleeve toward the stairs, shot him a look of pure contempt. “That is a terrible sentence.”

The figure at the threshold lifted its head.

Kofi felt the key jerk hard in his hand, almost wrenching free. He gritted his teeth.

“What is it?” he shouted over the noise of the station.

Anansi answered, voice tight with disgust and something worse. “An old crossing debtor. One of the ones the route was made to carry and never finished carrying.”

Kofi stared. “That’s not a person.”

“No,” said Anansi. “It used to be.”

The debtor reached one long arm through the seam. The air shivered around it. Wherever its hand passed, the tiles frosted over with a thin skin of pale residue.

Mara dragged the last of the conscious borrowers toward the stairs, then came back, refusing to stay safely away. “So we close it!”

“We can’t shut it with force now,” Anansi said. “It’s anchored.”

“Then unanchor it.”

Ekwu’s face tightened. “If the route collapses now, they will be trapped again.”

“Them?” Mara snapped. “You mean it.”

Ekwu looked at her, and for the first time all his authority felt thin enough to tear. “There were promises made.”

“Not to these people,” Mara said.

The debtor reached farther.

Kofi’s arm burned. The key was no longer merely tugging; it was pulling toward the opening with such insistence that he could feel it in his shoulder. The metal had gone hot. Patterns moved inside it like blood under skin.

Anansi’s eyes flicked to Kofi. “You need to choose.”

Kofi laughed once, breathless and furious. “I hate when gods say that.”

“Choose what?” Mara demanded.

Anansi pointed, not taking his eyes off the opening. “Turn the route fully and let it take what it was made to carry, or wrench the key back and seal it before more comes through.”

Kofi stared at him. “And the borrowers?”

Anansi’s jaw tightened. “They go home.”

“And if I don’t?”

Ekwu answered. “Then the old passage remains half open. That is worse.”

Mara had gotten the last borrower to the stairwell. She turned back, breathless, and looked at all of them as if measuring the distance between disaster and decision.

“Someone explain to me,” she said, “why the options are always terrible.”

No one answered fast enough.

That was when the debtor spoke.

Its voice did not emerge from a mouth so much as from the station walls themselves, all at once, layered and dry. “Return us.”

The words rolled over the platform like dust.

Mara froze.

Kofi felt the key twitch harder.

The debtor took another step forward and more of its body entered the light—ragged coat, bare ankles, a face worn smooth by crossing after crossing until identity had become a surface. There were other shapes behind it, clustered just beyond the seam.

Not one. Many.

A line of them waiting in the dark.

Ekwu’s expression cracked into something like horror. He had not expected so many.

Mara looked at him and understood. “What did you make this route for?”

Ekwu’s silence was answer enough again.

Anansi said quietly, “You made a gate for the unaccounted.”

Ekwu shut his eyes for a moment. “For the disappeared.”

Mara’s face changed. “That’s what this was for?”

No one spoke.

The debtor’s hand extended farther. Its fingers brushed the air near Kofi’s knuckles, and the key pulsed violently. He felt a memory flash through him—no, not a memory, an impression of a crowd at a platform that no longer existed, hands reaching, names being called, shoes against stone. Then the sensation vanished, leaving him gasping.

Ekwu said, very low, “They were supposed to come through and be given form again.”

Anansi barked a laugh with no humor in it. “And you expected to control that?”

“I expected a world that remembered its obligations.”

“That,” said Mara, voice shaking now with anger, “is not the same thing.”

The debtor reached again, and the station floor bucked. One of the lights went out. Then another. The pressure in the air became unbearable.

Kofi realized with sick clarity that the route was not opening into nowhere. It was opening into a place full of unfinished arrivals. A place where the forgotten had waited long enough to become something else. Ekwu had not only stolen a threshold. He had reopened a promise too large to contain.

Mara looked at the line of waiting figures in the dark and then back at Ekwu. “You used people as filler for a doorway to your own guilt.”

Ekwu flinched as if struck.

Anansi, who had been watching Kofi more than the route, said softly, “Now.”

Kofi looked at him.

“The key,” Anansi said. “You can still turn it back.”

Kofi stared down at the metal in his fist. It was scorching now. He could feel the pull up his arm all the way to the shoulder, and with it a strange current of voices—not words, but pressure, the sensation of many unfinished directions.

He looked at Mara. She was bleeding from a split lip he hadn’t noticed before, probably from the force of the recoil. She was still standing. Still watching him with the fierce, impatient trust of someone who had decided that if a thing could be fixed, it must be, and if not fixed, then at least not abandoned.

He looked at the borrowers. Several had reached the stairs now. They were human again in the worst and best way: frightened, confused, alive. Kofi’s chest tightened at the sight of them.

Then he looked at Ekwu.

The old god stood rigid at the lip of his own mistake, one ruined shoe, one intact, both of them suddenly absurd. He was not cruel in the simple sense. That was the worst part. He was someone who believed that making a forgotten thing visible justified everything done to get it there.

Kofi understood that kind of thinking. He had seen it in repairmen who cut corners to prove a point, in bosses who called sacrifice efficiency, in families that preserved damage because admitting it existed would mean changing the room around it.

He hated it.

But he also knew a thing about broken seams.

You could pull them tight and make them hold long enough to pretend.

Or you could open them properly and decide what went back in.

His hand turned the key a fraction.

The route shuddered.

The debtor in the opening raised its head, and behind it the line of waiting figures pressed forward. Kofi saw at last that some were wearing shoes like his own. Old trainers. School shoes. Work boots. Some were barefoot. Some had one shoe only.

Lost people, maybe.

Not dead exactly. Not whole either.

Mara saw his face change and shouted, “Kofi?”

He made his choice.

Not to let Ekwu have the gate.

Not to let the route stay half-open.

Not to let the old god use the station as an argument with history.

He turned the key back.

The sound was like a thousand laces being yanked tight at once.

The seam in Ekwu’s shoe flashed white, then snapped wider, then started to close in on itself as the route reversed. The debtor screamed—human, suddenly human, and the sound cut straight through the station. The line behind it rushed backward in a blur of shadow and reaching hands.

Anansi lunged forward, throwing both palms out. The air buckled around the opening.

Mara shouted for the last borrower to get up the stairs and ran back to help, grabbing another by the arm and hauling her bodily toward the exit.

Ekwu staggered as the key’s power tore out of him.

For one instant, he looked less like a god than a man who had built too much on a failing foundation and could not bear to watch it fall.

Then the route slammed shut.

Not sealed. Closed.

The light vanished. The pressure vanished. The station lights came back in a stuttering line, one by one, as though ashamed of having left.

Kofi dropped to one knee, the key falling from his hand and clattering across the platform. It was now just a small, ordinary piece of metal with a bent tooth and a dark stain at the loop.

The borrowers collapsed in stages—some weeping, some vomiting, some staring around in raw confusion. A few were already stumbling up the stairs under Mara’s direction. Others sat where they were, looking at their own shoes as if they had just returned from a country they could not name.

Anansi stood over the closed seam, breathing hard.

Ekwu had fallen backward against the tunnel wall. One of his sneakers was half split, the other intact. His face had gone gray with loss. Not defeat. Loss.

He looked up at Kofi, and for the first time in the story of his arrogance, he looked tired.

“You have closed it,” he said.

Kofi pushed himself to his feet slowly, every muscle aching. “Yes.”

“There were meant to be returns.”

“There were meant to be choices,” Kofi said.

Ekwu said nothing.

Mara came back down the platform, one hand braced on her side, breathing hard. She looked from Kofi to the god and then to the ruined shoe on Ekwu’s foot.

“Well,” she said hoarsely, “that could have gone better.”

Anansi let out one short laugh, surprised out of him.

Mara leaned over and picked up the bent key from the floor. She studied it for a moment, then handed it to Kofi. “Can you fix this?”

Kofi looked at the useless little thing in her palm.

Then at the people on the stairs.

Then at the closed seam in the world.

“Maybe,” he said. “But I don’t think it should open anything again.”

Ekwu watched them, and some part of his fury had cooled into something like understanding, though not enough to be called acceptance.

Anansi stepped toward him and, to Kofi’s surprise, crouched to inspect the damaged sneaker as a shoemaker might inspect a heel.

“You’ll need a proper repair,” Anansi said.

Ekwu’s mouth twitched. “From you?”

“No. From him.”

He nodded toward Kofi.

Kofi stared. “Absolutely not.”

Anansi straightened, smiling despite himself. “Then from someone with better patience than you.”

Mara snorted, then winced because it hurt. “Good luck finding that.”

Ekwu closed his eyes briefly. When he opened them again, the old hardness had not vanished, but it had been cut through by something more human. “I did not think,” he said, “that the road would answer you.”

Mara shrugged with one shoulder. “You keep underestimating the people on it.”

For a moment no one spoke.

Then, somewhere above them, the market began to open for the day. Metal shutters rose. Voices returned. Life resumed with its usual indifference to catastrophe.

The station beneath the market, though, felt changed. Not healed. But quieter. Less hungry.

Kofi looked at the broken sneaker in Ekwu’s hand and at the patch of floor where the route had closed. He could not have said what exactly had been saved. He only knew that the worst had not been allowed to keep happening.

That, for a repairman, was enough to count as sacred.

At the top of the stairs, Mara turned back once. “Are we done?”

Anansi looked at Kofi.

Kofi looked at the key.

Then at the shoes.

Then at the line of humans starting to find their feet again.

“No,” he said. “But we’re not in the same place anymore.”

And for the first time, that did not feel like a lie.
step_outputs.13:
By the time they got the last of the shaken borrowers out of the station, the market above was loud with ordinary life.

That was the strange mercy of it. No trumpets, no collapse of the sky, no public revelation that gods had been arguing under the vegetable stalls all morning. A woman haggled over tomatoes. Someone swept fish scales off the curb with a wet broom. A child shrieked because a pigeon had stolen half a bun. The world kept its small, stubborn motions.

Mara stood at the top of the station stairs with one hand on the rail and the other pressed against her side, breathing through pain that was already becoming a bruise. Her lip had split again while she’d been hauling people up, and every time she tasted blood she remembered the pressure in the tunnel.

Kofi was beside her, holding the bent key in a piece of cloth as if it might still bite.

Below them, Anansi and Ekwu remained in the platform hollow for a little longer.

Ekwu was not kneeling—Mara thought he would rather be struck by lightning—but he was sitting now, back against the tiled wall, one leg stretched out. The split shoe had been removed. His bare foot looked disconcertingly mortal in the cold station light. Anansi had the damaged sneaker in both hands and was turning it over with the concentrated irritation of a man unwillingly admiring a rival’s work.

Mara watched them for a moment and then said, “I can’t believe I’m saying this, but your friend should probably see someone about that.”

Kofi gave her a sideways look. “If you think he has a normal medical situation, you’ve learned nothing.”

She huffed a short laugh and immediately regretted it.

Anansi looked up. “He will need a repair.”

Ekwu’s expression was still hard, but dulled around the edges now. “I can walk.”

“That is not the point,” Anansi said.

“No?”

“No.”

Mara leaned on the rail and looked down at them. “I assume the point is not letting the world split open again.”

Anansi’s mouth twitched. “That is one point, yes.”

Kofi snorted. “You gods are exhausting.”

“Agreed,” Mara said.

Ekwu’s gaze lifted toward her. For a moment she thought he might make some cutting remark, but instead he only said, “You could have left.”

Mara blinked. “And let you all do whatever that was down there? Absolutely not.”

“That was foolish.”

“Yes,” she said. “I’m aware.”

He studied her a moment longer. Then, to her surprise, he inclined his head—small, formal, unwillingly sincere.

The gesture meant more because it was so reluctant.

Anansi noticed it and laughed softly. “Look at that. Progress.”

“Don’t start,” Ekwu said.

“I haven’t started.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I often do that when you suffer.”

Mara rolled her eyes. “Great. So this is your normal relationship.”

Kofi folded the key back into the cloth. “What happens now?”

That was the first real question nobody had answered.

The borrowers had been taken upstairs and sat in rows along the market wall, wrapped in spare jackets and blankets someone had found in a storage room. A few were crying. A few were staring at their hands. One kept trying to remove a shoe she was wearing and then stopping halfway through the motion as if she had forgotten why. Their keys, whatever they had been, were gone or hidden again or simply no longer relevant. The city around them remained unaware and therefore unhelpful.

Anansi stood. “Now,” he said, “we mend what can be mended.”

Kofi looked at the torn sneaker in his hand, then at the ruined seam on Ekwu’s other foot. “You say that like it’s easy.”

“It isn’t.”

“That’s better.”

Anansi glanced toward the market where people were still shopping in bright triangles of morning sunlight. “The route is closed, but not forgotten. That’s important.”

Ekwu pushed himself upright with some effort. “The threshold will remain unstable for a time.”

Mara’s face tightened. “Is that your apology?”

“No.”

“Thought not.”

Kofi crouched and picked up the damaged shoe from where it had been set aside. He turned it in his hands. The split seam looked worse in daylight. The canvas was worn to softness in places and rough in others. The sole had been repaired before, twice maybe. Whoever had done it had cared enough to keep the work functional, not beautiful.

He understood that.

“This wasn’t made to last forever,” he said.

Anansi’s eyebrows rose. “Few things are.”

Ekwu looked at the shoe in Kofi’s hands with something like grief. “It was meant to hold better.”

Kofi nodded once. “Then it needs a proper stitch.”

Mara glanced between them. “You’re really going to repair a divine shoe in the middle of a market?”

Kofi stood and looked at her with all the dead seriousness of his trade. “Where else?”

That almost made her smile.

So they stayed.

There was no mystical workshop, no hidden cathedral, no dramatic thunderstorm. Kofi set up a folding stool beside the wall. A shopkeeper, after one suspicious look at the group, brought a thermos of tea without asking questions. A woman with a produce crate set down a pair of scissors and a needle she’d borrowed from her cousin before the station collapse. Anansi, after briefly objecting to the tea as “too sweet,” drank two cups anyway. Mara sat with her back against a column and watched the god of roads and misdirection hold still long enough to let someone else mend what he could not.

Kofi worked by hand.

He trimmed the torn edge. Removed the useless thread. Laid new stitches with a thick waxed line that matched the old repairs more than the original construction. The damaged shoe rested on his knee as if it had chosen him. Every few minutes he paused, not because he was uncertain, but because he was listening to the material. The way it flexed. The way it resisted. The way it wanted to become a shoe again.

Anansi watched with an expression that was nearly reverent, which made him look absurd.

“Don’t stare,” Kofi said without looking up.

“I’m not staring.”

“You are.”

“I’m appreciating.”

“Same thing.”

Mara let her head fall back against the column. The market noise drifted around them in a warm, layered hum. She could hear a radio playing somewhere. A knife hitting a cutting board. The impatient bark of a vendor. The ordinary city—her city—moving around the edge of something it would never fully know.

After a while she asked, “So gods wear sneakers because they have to keep moving?”

Anansi looked at her, surprised into honesty by the quiet. “Sometimes.”

“Not always?”

“No.” He turned the tea cup in his hands. “Sometimes they wear them because they are trying to remember what it is to walk among people and not above them.”

Mara snorted softly. “That’s almost poetic.”

“I know. It annoys me too.”

Ekwu, seated against the wall with one bare foot tucked in, said, “It was never about fashion.”

Mara lifted an eyebrow. “That’s not the important part of the sentence.”

“No,” he said. After a beat, “It was about being able to cross without being excluded by the road.”

That surprised her.

He seemed to hear it in the silence and added, gruffly, “A shoe marks a boundary. Between body and ground. Between place and passage. Between what is endured and what is chosen.”

Kofi’s needle paused for just a second.

Mara looked at him. “You say that like you’ve thought about it.”

Ekwu’s expression closed again. “I have.”

Anansi gave a small, tired laugh. “He’s being philosophical because he lost an argument.”

“By your logic,” Ekwu replied, “you are constantly philosophical.”

That drew a real smile out of Mara despite herself.

The repaired shoe was finished near noon.

Kofi tied the last knot, tested the seam with his thumb, and set it down. “Not perfect,” he said.

Anansi raised an eyebrow. “You expect perfection from a sidewalk repair?”

“I expect function.”

Ekwu took the shoe from him carefully. He held it a moment as if weighing not just the object but the consequences of wearing it again. Then, with a grimace that might have been gratitude if it had been less dignified, he slipped it on.

It fit.

The relief in the station was almost physical. Mara could feel the air settle. Not because something grand had happened, but because one specific damage had been respected and answered.

Ekwu stood. Tested his footing. The shoe held.

He looked at Kofi. “You’re good.”

Kofi gave him a flat look. “I know.”

That got a startled sound from Mara and, unexpectedly, a low laugh from Anansi.

Ekwu’s mouth twitched, almost against his will.

Mara pushed herself upright and winced. “So what now? You all vanish into divine bureaucracy and leave me to explain why I missed half my deliveries?”

Anansi looked at her as if he might make a joke, then didn’t. “You go back to your routes.”

Mara looked at him. “That sounds disappointingly normal.”

“It is not,” he said. “You know that now.”

She did.

That was the thing. The city looked the same. The market was still the market. The tram still screamed around corners. But the world had acquired layers she could feel now, like hidden stitching under fabric. Doors were not only doors. Paths were not only convenience. Shoes were not only shoes.

She would never be able to unlearn that.

Kofi packed his tools. The bent key remained wrapped in cloth in his pocket, heavier than it should have been. He intended to keep it somewhere safe, though he suspected no safe place would be entirely safe enough.

Ekwu reached for the second shoe—his repaired one—then hesitated.

Mara saw that hesitation and understood something she would not have thought herself capable of understanding that morning: immortals could be embarrassed by their needs.

He cleared his throat. “The other one will need work too.”

Kofi looked up. “Obviously.”

Anansi sighed. “You could just say thank you.”

Ekwu gave him a look of pure offense. “No.”

That, more than anything, made Mara laugh.

They stood there under the market’s afternoon heat, four figures who should not have belonged together and now, briefly, did. Around them the city kept breathing. The borrowers were being taken to a clinic upstairs. Someone had begun handing out water. A child had wandered near the platform stairs and was now being hurried away by an alarmed aunt.

Mara looked at the repaired shoe in Ekwu’s hand and then at the pair on Anansi’s feet, one scuffed, one freshly dusted from the station floor.

For all the power in them, they were just shoes. Worn, repaired, laced, scuffed. Human in the parts that touched the ground.

And somehow that made the gods harder to dismiss.

At the edge of the market, a tram bell rang.

Mara took a breath, adjusted her courier bag on her shoulder, and started toward the stairs.

Behind her, Anansi called, “Mara.”

She turned.

He held something out. A shoelace, white and slightly frayed. Not the one from the tunnel. A different one. Ordinary, except that it felt colder in her hand when he placed it there.

“Keep that,” he said.

“What for?”

He smiled, and this time it was almost kind. “In case the road forgets you again.”

Mara closed her fingers around the lace.

When she looked back a second later, Anansi was already gone.

Ekwu was there for a moment longer, standing in the shade with one repaired shoe and one that would need repair soon enough. Then he too stepped away, not with thunder or ceremony, but simply into the crowd, as if he had always been part of it.

Kofi remained at the foot of the stairs, locking up his tools.

Mara glanced at him. “You believe any of that?”

He looked up, tired and dry and perfectly serious. “No.”

She waited.

Then he added, “That doesn’t mean it wasn’t real.”

Mara nodded once.

Above them the market moved on. Below them the station kept its silence. Between those two things, the city held.

And somewhere out there, on all the roads that mattered, gods kept walking in sneakers.
